new_statements.rule_in_words: LSFB is a signed language; no source gives a position for word (sign-internal) stress, and signs are treated as the syllable-sized unit. Prominence is described as a phrase/discourse-level, information-structure-driven property: contrastively focused signs are made prominent mainly by longer relative duration (deceleration), sign holds and weak-hand holds, and mouth articulations, with eyebrow/head/body-lean cues spanning the focus domain; large movement, spatial displacement and repetition (the ASL/DGS-type cues) play a minor role. Footnote 38 (p. 172) adds that manual prominence is also shaped by movement type, sign type and position in the signed unit, but these lexical/positional factors are not the primary drivers: prominence increases systematically with information structure. Sign languages in general are said to favour prominence at the end of phrases (p. 84, citing Nespor & Sandler 1999, Wilbur 1999, Crasborn et al. 2012).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable / not discussed. Prominence is scored as gradient (one point per co-occurring manual cue: relative duration >= 1, repetition, dominance reversal, change in vertical location, hold, mouth articulation; p. 109).
new_statements.exceptions: Movement repetition is rare in LSFB (4.8% of all signs, 7.5% of contrastively focused signs; p. 161), unlike RSL/NGT; holds are low-frequency but strongly associated with the 'discourse opposition' subtype of contrast and absent in 'selection' (p. 161). An alternative to repetition is the addition of a movement (p. 161).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the signed utterance/phrase in spontaneous and elicited dialogue from the LSFB Corpus (4 native signers in the 2022 case study; larger dataset in the thesis), not citation forms. The statement concerns prosodic prominence encoding contrastive focus, i.e. phrase-level accentuation; it says nothing about a fixed stress position inside a sign. Corroborating first-hand observation from a second saved file: Paligot 2018, p. 140 (pdf 143): 'La deuxième apparition du terme est accentuée : cela se marque par l'ampleur du mouvement, la durée de sa réalisation, et cela a également pour effet de neutraliser l'abaissement' (an accentuated token of the sign COMMENT shows larger movement, longer duration and no lowering), and p. 66 (pdf 69): a prosodic role of internal-movement repetition with more movement cycles at the end of sentences (phrase-final lengthening).
new_statements.identity_note: Sign language (Wallonia/Brussels, Belgium), glottocode lang1248 = ISO sfb. Not to be confused with Flemish Sign Language (VGT, vlaa1235) or LSF (fren1243). Both sources describe LSFB as used by native signers in the LSFB Corpus (UNamur); no dialect split. Positional word stress is not a category any source describes for this language; what is described is prosodic prominence under contrastive focus and phonetic 'accentuated' vs reduced forms of sign tokens.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing statement from Lombart 2026 (phrase-level prominence only, focus constituent moved to phrase-final position); the abstract adds the cue inventory (duration, holds, mouth articulations, manual-cue combinations). Abstract only, so no page-anchored body quote and no statement about placement within the phrase from this work itself. Lombart 2026 p. 170 (already held by the project) says its results 'support and refine preliminary observations from earlier stages of the current research (Lombart, 2022, 2023)', which is consistent with this compilation.
new_statements.rule_in_words: As far as the abstract shows, 'stress' in LSFB is prosodic prominence placed on the contrastive-focus constituent and cued by duration, holds, mouth articulations and combinations of manual cues; nothing indicates a positional word-level stress rule (sign-internal placement is not a category the work uses).
new_statements.identity_note: The work is about LSFB proper (Langue des signes de Belgique francophone), data from the LSFB Corpus (Meurant 2015), six native deaf signers, two tasks; no regional or dialectal sub-variety is singled out. Note that in this literature 'stress' means prosodic prominence on a sign or constituent marking (contrastive) focus, not a lexically fixed position within a sign, so the language has no word-stress rule of the catalog's positional kind.

new_statements.quote: The findings presented below suggest that LSFB signers employ a specific type of prosodic marking at the levels of stress and intonation to encode CF. Stress markers exhibit distinct variations in their frequency of use on CF and in the surrounding context. [...] Stress markers include variations in duration, mouth articulations, holds, and combinations of cues. They tend to make CF more prominent than the signs that precede or follow them. [p. 109] || [p. 110] Overall, the observations discussed so far indicate that there are no categorical but gradient differences between the markers used to encode CF and those occurring in the surrounding context.

new_statements.rule_in_words: LSFB is a sign language; this article has no positional or lexical word-stress category. 'Stress' here means prominence of contrastively focused (CF) signs relative to the non-contrastive signs before and after them, i.e. a discourse/phrase-level, information-structural prominence: CF signs are longer (mean 662 ms vs 458 ms before and 424 ms after, p <.001), carry holds and mouth articulations significantly more often, and combine three or more manual cues more often; vertical location in space shows no significant pattern; dominance reversals and prosodic movement repetitions are more frequent on CF but too rare (about 5% of signs) to test. Nonmanual 'intonation' cues (body leans, head movements; not eyebrows) differ in form on CF and layer with one another. Differences are gradient, not categorical, and no single marker is obligatory or specific to CF.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none (not a category in this work)
new_statements.exceptions: Eyebrow movements show no CF-specific difference (lesser role in LSFB); location/height variation not significant; dominance reversal and repetition untested for rarity; no marker is CF-specific or used in all cases, contra claims for NGT/LSC (dominance reversal, body leans, mouth articulations); stress and intonation cues are interconnected at the nonmanual level rather than strictly manual=stress / nonmanual=intonation (contra Sandler 2012).
new_statements.identity_note: LSFB (Langue des signes de Belgique francophone), data from the LSFB Corpus (Meurant 2015, Université de Namur), six native deaf signers in spontaneous dyadic tasks; no regional variety distinguished.

No word-internal stress position is stated.
